title: The indwelling presence
hook: the presence of God in the world, often pictured as feminine

segments.voice: Yesterday, endurance: Netzach and Hod, the two legs that walk, resting on Yesod, the foundation. Your line was endure. Did the small unfinished thing get its plain last step? Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

"And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them." That's God speaking to Moses in the book of Exodus, in the desert, before a single tent pole has gone up. Some readers have stopped on the last words. Not that I may dwell in it, in the building. Among them. In the people. A tent of cloth and wood, carried from camp to camp, and the promise is that God will live in the middle of all that walking and arguing and cooking. The rabbis gave that nearness a name that echoes the verse's own word for dwell. Today's word.
screen: `MAKE ME A SANCTUARY.` → `NOT IN IT. AMONG THEM.` → `GOD IN THE MIDDLE OF THE CAMP.`

segments.voice: Shechinah. The indwelling presence of God. Turn it four ways. First, the rabbis' word. They use it to speak of God close at hand. Pirkei Avot teaches that when people sit together and their talk is words of Torah, the Shechinah rests among them. Not in a temple. At a table. Second, it goes where the people go. The Talmud says that wherever Israel was exiled, the Shechinah went into exile with them. The presence doesn't stay behind in a ruined building. It packs its bags. Third, Kabbalah. Remember yesterday's promise: where everything lands. The last of the ten lights is Malchut, kingship, the one that touches the world, and kabbalists identify it with the Shechinah. Every light above flows down into her. And notice the her. Kabbalists picture the Shechinah as feminine: a queen, a bride, sometimes a mother. Some Jews welcome the Sabbath on Friday night with songs that greet a bride and a queen, and kabbalists heard the Shechinah in those images. Fourth, the longing. In kabbalistic teaching, the Shechinah is in some sense separated, in exile, and human deeds of Torah, prayer and kindness help reunite her with the Holy One above. A Jewish reader might hear that as a job description: every good act, a little homecoming. In this teaching, the God without end, from a few days ago, is also the presence at the table.
screen: `PRESENCE AT A TABLE.` · `SHE GOES INTO EXILE TOO.` · `MALCHUT: WHERE THE LIGHTS LAND.` · `GOOD DEEDS AS HOMECOMING.` · then, large: `PRESENCE DWELLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice presence in a room. Wherever you are, settle, and breathe. Let your eyes move slowly around the space. The light on the wall. The chair. The sounds from outside. If there are other people near, notice them too, without looking at them too hard. Then let your attention rest not on any one thing, but on the whole room, the space everything is sitting in. If you pray, you can hold the words from Exodus: that I may dwell among them. If you don't, just notice being here. The bell holds the time.
Shechinah. The indwelling presence of God, among the people and with them in exile; in Kabbalah, Malchut, pictured as a queen and a bride. Today's word.
Your line: presence dwells. Today, when you sit down to eat with someone, or talk, pause for one breath and notice the space between you. Day one thousand one hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Jews speak of the Shechinah in prayer and study, and some families, following a custom of the kabbalists, sing to welcome the Sabbath as a bride and queen on Friday evening.

fork.setup: God tells Moses: make Me a sanctuary. where does the verse say God will dwell?
options: in the building, and nowhere else.
fork.reveal: "that I may dwell among them." some readers stop on those words: in the people, not only in the tent.

original.note: Hebrew: the indwelling presence of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mystical name for a goddess.
what it means: the presence of the one God dwelling among people; in Kabbalah, Malchut, pictured as feminine.
what a scholar hears: the rabbinic word echoing veshachanti in Exodus 25:8, Pirkei Avot 3:6, the Shechinah in exile in Megillah 29a, and Malchut as Shechinah in the kabbalists.

sources.quoted: And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.

notes: Exodus 25:8 quoted from JPS 1917; please confirm exact wording.
The link between Shechinah and the verb shachan (to dwell) is a root claim; stated as 'built from the same Hebrew root as dwell'. Please confirm.
Pirkei Avot 3:6 (or 3:2 depending on numbering) paraphrased; the numbers in the mishnah (ten, five, three, two, one) are left out.
Megillah 29a paraphrased: wherever Israel was exiled, the Shechinah went with them.

Kabbalistic identification of Malchut with Shechinah, feminine imagery, Shechinah in exile and its reunion through human deeds: general teaching, paraphrased. The Friday-night bride and queen songs (e.g. Lecha Dodi) are mentioned without naming or dating them.
Trapdoor floor 1 'a mystical name for a goddess' is a misunderstanding the lesson corrects; please confirm it isn't unfair.
